facts.statement: The piopio (Turnagra) was an extinct genus of passerine birds endemic to New Zealand.
facts.quote: The piopio or turnagras are an extinct genus of passerine birds in the family Oriolidae, that were endemic to New Zealand.

facts.statement: Although sometimes called New Zealand thrushes, the piopio only superficially resembled the thrush family.
facts.quote: Sometimes described as New Zealand thrushes, the piopio had only a coincidental, passing resemblance to the thrush family.

facts.statement: The genus Turnagra was placed in the family Oriolidae because the birds were closely related to figbirds.
facts.quote: The genus Turnagra was then placed in the family Oriolidae after it was determined that the piopio were closely related to the figbirds.

facts.statement: The piopio were split into separate North Island and South Island species in 2012.
facts.quote: The piopio were formerly considered to be a single species until split into separate North and South Island species in 2012.

facts.statement: The species name Turnagra tanagra was based on a mistaken belief that the bird was related to American tanagers.
facts.quote: The North Island's Turnagra tanagra was so named because it was thought to be related to the tanagers of the Americas.

facts.statement: The piopio lived during the Holocene epoch.
The genus Turnagra existed from the Late Pleistocene to the Holocene, between 0.129 and 0 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Late Pleistocene to Holocene (0.129 to 0 million years ago)

facts.statement: The piopio frequented the undergrowth and forest floor.
facts.quote: They frequented the undergrowth and forest floor.

facts.statement: The piopio built well-constructed cup nests in trees a few meters off the ground, laying two to four eggs.
facts.quote: Their nests were well constructed cups placed in trees a few metres from the ground, in which two to four eggs were laid.

facts.statement: The piopio were omnivorous, eating insects, spiders, fruit, and oats.
facts.quote: They were omnivorous, with records of them hawking for insects over a river, as well as eating spiders, fruit and oats.

facts.statement: The South Island piopio was last recorded in 1905.
facts.quote: The South Island piopio was last recorded in 1905.

facts.statement: Some researchers have suggested a relationship between the piopio and the whistler family (Pachycephalidae).
facts.quote: A relationship has also been suggested with the whistlers (Pachycephalidae).
